metric.why: Rates rising after a decade of decline is the clearest market evidence that demand outran supply. Rate data is compiled by commercial research firms listed in the directory below; it is not republished here.
metric.definition: Market rate per kilowatt per month for leased capacity, the price signal for scarcity in each metro.

reading.body:
After a decade of falling rates, colocation rental prices have begun rising, the most direct market signal that AI compute demand now exceeds available supply.

Colocation rates measure what customers pay per kilowatt per month for leased data center capacity. When these prices fall, supply is abundant relative to need. When they rise, operators can charge more because alternatives are scarce. The reversal from decline to growth indicates the market has shifted. This matters because colocation is where most companies without their own infrastructure run AI workloads. If the price of renting compute goes up, training and inference become more expensive, which constrains who can afford to scale AI systems.

The data shows the price signal but not its magnitude or regional variation. It does not explain how much rates have risen, in which geographies, or whether rises are temporary or sustained. It also does not isolate the demand from AI versus other compute workloads. The rate increase is consistent with the thesis that power and buildings have become binding constraints on AI scaling, but rate data alone cannot distinguish between insufficient capacity, insufficient power supply, or insufficient grid connections.
